quest.mebahelrpgrquest.barrow_that_breat: A Watch Against the Dead
The tower has gone silent, but the village is still exposed. Help build a small watchtower before the dead come looking for the horn you silenced.
The elder is waiting near the edge of the village, staring at the road that leads back to the tower.
The tower is silent now.
Silent, yes. Safe, no. If the dead heard that horn once, they may come looking for the hand that stopped it.
You think they will attack the village?
I think the dead do not forgive interruption. They were being called to something, and you broke the first call.
What do you want me to do?
Help us raise a watchtower. Stone for the base, timber for the frame, fences for the top, and a lantern high enough for every frightened soul to see.
You want me to build it?
The guards are afraid, and the masons are pretending not to hear me. But if you build it, they may remember they have spines.
The watchtower still stands. I heard the bell, then the arrows, then the dead at the gates. Tell me the silence afterward was yours.
The dead came for the village.
Then the horn was not alone. Something heard it. Something sent them to test us.
The watchtower held.
Because you built it, and because you stood there when others would have hidden behind doors.
They had archers.
Archers? Then these were no wandering corpses. Someone is arranging the dead like soldiers.
What now?
Now we stop guessing. The tablet named soldiers, but not the king. We need the one who carved that name away.
Take this. The village has a watchtower now, but I fear we have only lit a candle in front of a tomb.
The watchtower still burns at night. Some sleep easier for it. I do not.
Horn-Drawn Draugr
A draugr staggers from the darkness, drawn toward the new watchlight.
Road-Woken Draugr
Another dead warrior answers the broken horn's memory.
Frost-Mouthed Draugr
A third corpse comes through the dark, frost spilling from its jaw.
Gate-Scraping Draugr
A heavier draugr lumbers toward the village gate, dragging its axe across the ground.
Barrow Archer
A draugr archer appears beyond the torchlight, bow already drawn toward the watchtower.
Frost-Eyed Archer
A second archer takes position farther out, using the dark between houses as cover.
Whispers Below
I need someone brave enough to go to the old Draugr Tower. Something inside it has started calling to the dead, and if that call spreads, this village will not survive the next night.
Come closer. I would rather not say this where every frightened ear in the village can hear me.
What happened?
The old Draugr Tower has started making sounds again. Not wind. Not stone settling. A horn, deep under the earth.
A horn?
Aye. And after it sounds, something answers from below. The dead are not wandering anymore. They are listening.
Why has no one gone there?
Because the last guard who reached the tower came back without his shield, without his sword, and without a single word left in him.
What do you want me to do?
Go to the tower first. See if the old stories are true. If something inside is waking the draugr, break it before the call spreads.
You are back. Tell me quickly. Does the tower still call to the dead?
The tower is silent.
Then you have done more than clear old stone. You have stopped the first horn before the rest could answer.
There was a spawner inside.
A cursed anchor, then. The dead were being gathered, not merely awakened.
You think there are more?
I fear it. Towers do not wake alone. Somewhere beneath the hills, something older is giving orders.
What kind of orders?
The kind only the buried obey. The kind carved into tomb walls and sealed behind claw-locked doors.
Take this. You bought us time, but I fear the tower was only the first stone to stir.
The tower is silent now, but I still do not trust the quiet.
The Name of the Dead King
The tablet you found names every buried warrior except one. I need you to find the dead scribe who erased that name and decide whether his silence deserves death or mercy.
The elder has not slept. The cracked tablet lies before him, covered in candle wax and shaking shadows.
What did the tablet say?
It was a burial record. Names of warriors, oathmen, shield-brothers... all bound to one king.
One king?
That is the trouble. His title remains, but his name was carved out. Someone wanted him forgotten.
Who erased it?
A death-scribe. A draugr priest trained to bind names to tombs and oaths to bones.
And you think he still exists?
I think the dead do not forget their duties. Find him in the crypt, and make him speak. But listen carefully before you decide what he deserves.
You have returned. Tell me what happened in the crypt.
The king's name was Kjorvund Black-Crowned.
Then the old fear has a name again. I had hoped never to hear it spoken aloud.
Vahruk erased the name to weaken him.
A death-scribe who betrayed his king to save the living... that is not the tale I expected.
He said the Bastion guards an Oath-Seal.
Then the seal is the true command. Not a relic. Not treasure. A voice waiting for a dead army.
What if I killed him?
Then we go forward with blood on the answer. It may be necessary. It may also be exactly what the dead king wanted.
Whether you judged him or spared him, the path now leads to the Bastion. Find the seal before Kjorvund's army remembers how to march.
The death-scribe has spoken. I still cannot decide whether he was a monster, a coward, or the only reason we are alive.
Vahruk the Name-Eater
The death-scribe has risen inside the old crypt. He carries the name that was cut from the tablet.
The draugr wight turns slowly. Its jaw opens with the sound of stone dragged across stone.
A traitor and a monster are still both dead.
You betrayed him to save the living. That is enough.
Vahruk raises his blade. The crypt answers with the scrape of waking bones. If you want the king's name, you will take it through blood.
You lower your weapon. Vahruk stares at you as if mercy is more painful than steel.
Then hear the rest. The Bastion does not guard treasure. It guards the Oath-Seal. Take it, and the king's command breaks. Take it wrongly, and every buried throat will answer.
You spared the death-scribe? Then the story is worse than I feared. If he betrayed his own king to save the living, perhaps the dead have carried more truth than we did.
Oathbound Draugr
Are you Vahruk?
Vahruk was the hand. The chisel. The silence. I carved the king from memory.
What king?
The black-crowned one. The oath-bound one. The one whose army still waits beneath the frost.
Say his name.
Kjorvund Black-Crowned. King of the sealed host. Break his oath, or kneel when he rises.
Why erase his name?
Because I was ordered to preserve him. So I betrayed him instead. A king without a name cannot command. A dead army without command can only dream.
You erased him to stop him?
I damned myself to weaken him. Every age calls me traitor. Every corpse calls me coward. Yet the world still breathes because I carved one name away.
The Bastion Oath
Vahruk is dead, and whatever truth he carried was torn from him by force. Now the Bastion waits, already warned by blood. Find the oath-seal, take it, and survive whatever answers.
The elder watches the blood dry on the cracked tablet. Whatever Vahruk knew, you took the king's name from him with steel.
Vahruk gave me the name before he died.
Then we know enough to be afraid. Kjorvund Black-Crowned was not merely buried. He was contained.
He chose to fight.
Perhaps. Or perhaps the dead king wanted him silenced before he could say more.
You think killing him was a mistake?
I think some truths bleed when cut. Now we go to the Bastion with only half the warning.
Then what do I do?
Find the oath-seal and take it. If the dead rise to stop you, cut through them before the Bastion wakes fully.
You have it? The seal... and by your wounds, the Bastion did not let you take it quietly.
The dead rose the moment I took it.
Then Vahruk's death warned them. The Bastion knew you were coming before your hand touched the seal.
Hroldan rose with fire in his armor.
Kjorvund's inner guard. The old songs said they burned beneath their burial plates. I had hoped the songs lied.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.grey_banner_3_the: And now?
Now they are closer.
The dead are gone. The gate still stands. No one is cheering.
They came because of the truth.
No. They came because the truth was left too long in the dark.
Will the village admit what happened?
Not today. Maybe not this generation. But children ask why banners fly. That is enough.
The village lost its clean story, but kept its walls. That is more mercy than it gave Harvald.
The grey banner still flies. Some spit when they pass it. Some bow.
Wall-Called Draugr
Gate-Forsaken Draugr
Grey Banner Dead
Mud-Wall Draugr
The Last Man on the Wall
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.saint_of_rot_1_as: Do not call it cursed before you have watched fever take a child by inches. If there is ash left in that ruined church, bring it to me.
The healer keeps her hands folded, but grey dust has settled beneath her nails.
You are using ash as medicine?
Medicine is whatever keeps a child breathing until morning.
The ruined church beyond the old road. Beneath the altar, sealed in a cracked urn.
So does fever, when it takes a house one bed at a time.
What do you want from me?
Bring more ash. Judge me after the dying stop begging.
You found it. Good. Do not look at me like that. I know what it smells like.
Then the old priest knew where mercy was buried.
Or where something cursed was hidden.
If curses lower fever and ease pain, the gods should be ashamed of themselves.
One pinch in water, and the shaking stops. Tell me what curse does better work than mercy.
The ash is almost gone again. The fever is not.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.saint_of_rot_2_th: The Saved
He was dying yesterday. Today he breathes, speaks, and remembers names no living man taught him. Tell me whether I saved him or only delayed the grave.
The healer waits beside a man tied to a chair. His eyes are open, but his lips move to a prayer no one taught him.
Is he dangerous?
He was dying yesterday. Today he can stand, speak, and remember names that are not his.
You did this to him.
I kept him alive. If the price comes due, then say it plainly. But do not pretend death was cleaner.
What do you want?
Speak to him. If there is still a man in there, find him. If there is not, be quicker than the fever was.
Edran is dead. I asked for mercy and got certainty. Perhaps that is all this village deserves.
He was changing.
Everyone sick enough changes. Pain makes strangers of us before magic ever gets the chance.
The ash is not safe.
No. But it works. That is why this is cruel.
Go to the church. Burn the altar, break the urns, do whatever righteous people do after the desperate have already paid.
Edran's chair is empty. The healer has not moved it.
Edran the Saved
Edran waits near the healer's house. He is breathing. He is speaking. Neither of those things means he is safe.
The sick man turns toward you. His voice is his own for a moment, then older.
You lower your weapon. Edran exhales like a man who expected mercy to hurt more.
Take me to the church. If the bell wants my voice, let it ask while I am awake.
You spared him? Then you have more faith in that thing wearing Edran's face than I do.
The ash has taken too much of you.
You are still here. That matters.
You did it. Then the ash can heal flesh, but not what it invites inside.
Do you know what is happening to you?
I was dying. Then I was not. Now I dream with someone else's mouth.
What do you hear?
A bell under the church. It rings when I sleep. It counts the names of people who are not dead yet.
Are you still Edran?
Ask me while I still know the answer.
Do you want me to end it?
I want to see one more sunrise as myself. If that is too much to ask, then be quick.
Ash-Sick Villager
Take me back to the church. I want to hear the bell while I still know which voice is mine.
The ash in Edran's veins stirs. Sick shapes stumble from the dark, answering the bell beneath the stones.
Edran closes his eyes. Whatever was speaking through him waits.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.saint_of_rot_3_co: Condemn the Church
If Edran's death bought you certainty, spend it well. Go to the ruined church, board the doors, mark the stones, and leave me with the fever you call natural.
The healer does not look at you when she speaks.
The ash has to end.
Then end the road to it. Board the church, mark it, and make sure even desperate hands know not to enter.
You hate me for this.
No. Hate is simple. I envy you. You can leave after choosing who dies.
Why board it up instead of burning it?
Because people will call a burnt church tragedy. A boarded church is a warning.
You knew it was wrong.
I knew it was working. That is worse.
The church is boarded. The doors are marked. The fever came back before dawn.
No one will use the ash again.
No. Now they will just stand outside the boards and wonder how many planks a life is worth.
The dead will stop calling.
Good. Then the living can die in their own voices.
You know it had to be done.
I know many things. Knowing them has not made me kinder.
You could not keep using it.
And now I get to watch what happens when I stop. Do not dress that as comfort.
Two houses lost children this morning. The church is quiet, yes. So are they.
The ruined church is boarded now. The healer no longer prays where people can hear her.
Ash-Preserved Dead
A dead thing rises through the ruined church, its ribs packed with grey ash.
Altar-Fed Draugr
Another corpse pulls itself from the church floor, drawn by the sound of hammering wood.
Grey Saint's Dead
The last of the ash-fed dead staggers forward, wearing prayer like rot.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.saint_of_rot_3_pr: Take me back to the ruined church. I want to hear the bell while I still know which voice is mine.
Edran keeps his hands pressed over his ears, though no bell is ringing.
Yes. But now it is afraid.
No. Whatever is holding the rope.
If I fall, do not carry me. Drag me. I would rather arrive ashamed than arrive dead.
The ruined church is quiet. I can breathe without borrowing someone else's mouth.
No. But it has stopped pretending to be mine.
Not a saint. Not a demon either. Something worse. Something useful.
It kept me alive. That is what makes it dangerous.
I do not know if I am saved. But I am still the one speaking. That is more than I had.
The church road is quieter now. I still hear the bell, but it waits its turn.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.saint_of_rot_4_th: The Bell Under Stone
There is no saint beneath the church. There is a bell that teaches the dying how to remain useful to the dead. Help me silence it before someone desperate calls that mercy again.
Edran stands before the broken altar. His hands shake, but his voice is finally his own.
You know what is under the altar now?
I know what it wanted me to become. Not dead. Not alive. Preserved. Useful. Grateful.
Why call it a bell?
Because it rings without sound. It pulls on the names of the sick until they answer in their sleep.
The healer thought it was a miracle.
Maybe it was. That is the cruel part. A thing can save your body and still steal the rest.
What do you want to do?
Break it while I still hate it. If I wait too long, I may start thanking it.
The bell is silent. I am still breathing. For once, those two things do not feel like enemies.
Are you still yourself?
For now. That is not nothing.
The ash cannot be used again.
Then someone will die cursing us for being right.
The healer will hate this.
She should. Hate is easier to carry than empty hands.
Was this mercy?
Mercy is what people call the knife after it cuts the right throat.
I still live. The village lost its miracle. The dead lost their bell. I do not know who won, and that may be the most honest ending we get.
The ruined church is quiet. No one agrees what that quiet cost.
The Bell-Keeper
The Bell-Keeper rises beneath the ruined altar. Its mouth opens, and every sickbed in the village seems to breathe through it.
Ash-Preserved Dead
Grey Ash Thrall
Almost-Saved Dead
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.barrow_that_breat: More draugr came than expected.
Blood calls loudly in old tombs. Perhaps the death-scribe's silence was protecting us more than we understood.
But the seal is ours.
Yes. And perhaps that is all history will remember. Not how cleanly it was done, only that someone survived doing it.
You broke the seal as you broke the scribe: with steel and certainty. Perhaps that is what saved us. Perhaps that is simply what the dead understand best.
The Bastion is silent now, but sometimes I wonder if Vahruk's warning died too soon.
Oath-Seal of Kjorvund
Hroldan, Blood-Woken Oathkeeper
The oath-seal turns cold in your hand. Blood-dark fire spills through the Bastion stones, and Hroldan rises as if Vahruk's death was the final horn.
Blood-Scribe Wight
A wight claws itself from the dust, whispering Vahruk's name like an accusation.
Black-Crowned Wight
A second wight answers the seal's call, blocking the way back through the ruin.
Blood-Woken Draugr
A draugr lurches from the shadows, drawn by the violence that opened the path.
Bastion Dead
Another corpse answers the broken oath with rusted steel.
Oath-Marched Draugr
A third draugr marches forward as if commanded by a voice under the stone.
The Bastion Oath
Vahruk revealed the truth: the Bastion guards not treasure, but the command that lets Kjorvund's dead army rise. Take the oath-seal carefully, and break the king's voice without becoming its echo.
The elder reads Vahruk's warning again and again. The death-scribe did not protect the king. He crippled him.
Vahruk betrayed Kjorvund to save the living.
Then perhaps history buried the wrong villain. Or perhaps the dead have had centuries to make cowards sound noble.
He said the Bastion guards the Oath-Seal.
Then the seal is the king's voice. Not a relic, not a trophy. A command waiting for a throat.
Can we destroy it?
Maybe. But first you must take it from the Bastion. If Vahruk spoke truth, the guardians will rise when the seal leaves its rest.
What should I do when they come?
Do not answer hatred with hatred. Break the guardians, take the seal, and bring it back before the king's name becomes a banner again.
You have it? Good. Set it here carefully. I do not want that thing hearing its own name spoken aloud.
The guardians rose when I touched it.
Then Vahruk told the truth. The seal was not stored in the Bastion. It was enthroned there.
Hroldan seemed commanded, not hateful.
That may be the worst part. Some monsters choose evil. Others are simply never released from obedience.
The wights tried to keep me from leaving.
Scribes of the oath, perhaps. Dead hands keeping a dead king's voice intact.
What happens to the seal now?
We bury it where no crown, claw, or king can reach it. And we remember that even the dead can resist a tyrant.
You broke the seal without becoming its echo. Vahruk was right: some oaths are not defeated by hatred, but by refusing to obey them.
The Bastion is silent now. If Vahruk still walks somewhere in that dark, perhaps he finally knows his betrayal mattered.
Oath-Seal of Kjorvund
Hroldan, Oathkeeper of Kjorvund
The oath-seal turns cold in your hand. Hroldan rises from the dark, not enraged, but commanded.
Ash-Bound Wight
A draugr wight claws its way from the Bastion dust, drawn by the stolen oath-seal.
Black-Crowned Wight
A second wight answers the seal's call, blocking the way back through the ruin.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.grave_that_still_: The Dead Guard
A villager heard of a draugr walking the old road near a ruined tower. It follows travelers, but does not strike unless threatened.
You killed it. Good. But if it remembered the road, then something taught a corpse to wait there.
Take this. If more dead things start remembering, come back before the village forgets how to sleep.
The old road is quiet now. I wish that felt like peace.
Svanir the Road-Forgotten
A draugr stands near the old tower road. It carries a sword, watches the path, and has not attacked yet. Find out whether it is a threat before fear makes the choice for us.
The draugr lowers its blade slightly. Its voice is dry, broken, but not empty.
You lower your weapon. The draugr stares at the village road as if seeing it for the first time in centuries.
The bell. I remember the bell now. Not all of it, but enough to walk.
You spared it? Then either you found mercy, or you brought us a worse problem. I hope you know which.
Whatever you were, you are too dangerous now.
I will not cut down a memory.
So the dead guard is gone. I should be relieved, but a corpse that remembers a road does not happen by accident.
Can you understand me?
Understand... enough. Road. Bell. Snow in the mouth. I was ordered to guard. I guarded the wrong fear.
Who are you?
Svanir. No. Shield-hand. Road-guard. Coward. The words change when I try to hold them.
Why do you follow travelers?
Small hand. Red cloak. Bell on the braid. She held my cloak when the dark had teeth.
Who was she?
My charge. My oath. My shame. I remember the scream better than the name.
Oath-Called Dead
You spared me. There is a road in my head, and a bell at the end of it. Walk with me. If I remember what I was, I may remember where my oath broke.
The tower road exhales frost. Dead hands rise from the old stones, drawn by the mercy you showed.
The draugr watches the road in silence. Whatever memory stirred in it fades before it can become words.
Beneath the Bell
The spared draugr remembers a village bell and asks you to walk with him toward the place where his oath first broke.
Svanir keeps his sword low. His gaze is fixed beyond the road, toward a bell only he seems to hear.
You remember the village?
Bell. Smoke. Snow against the door. A child holding my cloak because the dark had teeth.
The bell means something to you.
She had a little bell tied to her braid. I told her it would help me find her if the snow grew thick.
Did it?
No. When the screaming began, I heard it behind me. I kept running anyway.
You want to go back there?
I need to hear the bell and not mistake it for her dying.
Then we go together.
If I falter, do not forgive me. If the dead come for me, do not let them take the village with them.
Svanir stands beneath the bell. He does not look at the dead around him. He looks at the villagers who are still alive.
The dead came for you.
No. They came for the oath still wrapped around my bones.
You held your ground this time.
I heard the bell and did not run. That is not redemption. But it is the first honest thing I have done in centuries.
Do you remember the child's name?
Alva. Her name was Alva. I had no right to forget it.
What now?
Now I find the thing that kept my shame useful.
The villagers live, and Svanir remembers the name he buried under fear. But something still holds his oath from the Bastion.
The bell no longer sounds like a scream. Not always.
Oath-Hunter Draugr
A draugr steps from the dark, staring past you toward Svanir.
Road-Caller Draugr
Another corpse answers the old oath, dragging its axe through the village dirt.
Bell-Hating Draugr
A third draugr turns its skull toward the bell, hatred burning in its empty eyes.
Frost-String Archer
A draugr archer appears beyond the torchlight, bow already drawn toward the villagers.
Grave-Road Archer
A second archer takes position farther out, using the village dark as cover.
The Grave That Would Not Rest
Walk with me to Alva's grave. I have carried my fear longer than I carried my shield, and I would set one of them down before I follow another road.
Svanir stands beneath the village bell, one hand closed around a small rusted charm.
You remembered her name.
Alva. I thought saying it would make the memory softer. It made it sharper.
What do you need now?
Her grave. I remember where they buried her. Or where they said they did. I never went to see it.
Why not?
Because a grave cannot be lied to. Villagers can. Priests can. Even the dead can, for a while. But stone remembers weight.
You want me to take you there?
Yes. If the old dead rise to judge me, let them. I have been running from children and corpses long enough.
This is the place. I remember the stone. I remember refusing to look at it.
The dead rose when you arrived.
Good. Let them see me. Let them know I came back without excuses.
Were they guarding her?
No. They were guarding the truth I buried with her.
What would you tell Alva?
That I ran. That I lived long enough to regret it. That death did not make me brave. Someone else had to do that.
She was only a child.
Yes. That is the part no oath can polish clean.
And now?
Now I leave the bell here. If she hears anything of me, let it be this silence, not my excuses.
What will you do after?
Walk. Guard. Stand when standing matters. If you will have me, I would rather carry my shame beside the living than bury it again with the dead.
Svanir places the rusted bell on the grave and rises without looking away. His sword is no longer a chain. It is a choice.
Alva's grave is quiet. Svanir still hears the bell, but now it sounds like farewell.
Grave-Witness Draugr
A draugr rises from the cold earth, not to defend treasure, but to stand witness.
Oath-Witness Draugr
Another dead warrior turns toward Svanir, as if the grave itself has called for judgment.
The Child's Last Witness
A wight steps from beside the grave. Its empty face turns not to you, but to the dead guard who finally came back.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.grey_banner_1_the: The Fallen Wall
Go to the ruined wall and listen before you swing. If Harvald was a coward, end him. If the village lied, bring me something uglier than a clean story.
So Harvald is dead for good. The wall can keep its secrets now.
Take this. The village will sleep easier if no one asks what the dead were trying to say.
The fort is quiet. I prefer quiet ruins.
Harvald Grey-Banner
The old fort still has a dead captain in it. The village says he failed his watch. Go see if the corpse agrees.
The wight stands beneath a broken wall, one hand resting on a banner pole with no banner left.
You lower your weapon. Harvald looks past you, toward the village, as if waiting for a gate to open centuries too late.
Then carry the truth. Not for me. For the wall. For the men whose names were buried under someone else's fear.
You spared him? Then you brought back more than a ghost. You brought back an accusation.
Whatever the truth was, you are still a danger.
The village should hear what happened here.
Then the fort is quiet. Good. Maybe some silences are worth more than old accusations.
Are you Harvald?
Harvald held the wall. Harvald watched the village gates close. Harvald died listening to the living pray he would stay blamed.
The village says you abandoned them.
The living often give the dead clean names for dirty work. Coward. Traitor. Failure. Easier than saying 'we shut the gate.'
Why stay here?
Because the banner fell before the truth did. I will not let both rot in the mud.
What do you want?
Raise the grey banner where they can see it. Let the village remember who bled outside their walls.
Wall-Called Dead
Raise the banner. Let the wind say what the living would not.
The broken wall groans. Dead hands rise where the old watch once stood.
Harvald turns back to the wall. The wind takes his words before they become a plea.
quest.mebahelrpgrquest.grey_banner_2_bur: Burn the Lie
Go back to the fort. Harvald is dead, but dead men leave names behind. Bring me the roll from the wall, and I will decide whether those names still need speaking.
The elder looks relieved, but not innocent.
Harvald is dead.
Then perhaps the road is safer.
You do not sound convinced.
A dead man with a grievance is rarely ended by one more blade.
What do you want now?
The old fort kept a roll of names. Soldiers posted there, villagers sheltered behind them, debts no one paid. Find it.
You want proof.
I want control of what proof survives.
That sounds like burying the truth.
Truth buried badly becomes a corpse. Truth buried well becomes peace.
You found the roll. Give it here before someone younger and angrier learns how to read old ink.
There were names on it.
Names are dangerous. They turn dead men into fathers, brothers, sons. Easier to mourn a wall than the people left on it.
The village abandoned them.
The village survived them.
That is not the same thing.
No. It is merely the version that still has children running in the streets.
What will you do with the roll?
